ple_read_fusion.question: is the HIP PLE row gather fused the way our Vulkan one is?
ple_read_fusion.answer: NO, and measured: 3245 bytes of physical disk read per PLE row lookup against a 90-byte row (36.1x amplification, 0.79 of the 4096-byte page ceiling). 55485-token prefill = 2747.7 MB read, 887760 lookups, ~12.6K IOPS. Disk bandwidth is not the limit (39 MB/s); the count of round trips and the cache waste are.
ple_read_fusion.vulkan_contrast: our Vulkan path (OPTIMIZATION.md) sorts, dedups AND merges adjacent ranges in llama-mmap.cpp, then batch-prefetches pages: measured ~63 KiB/fault down to ~8 KiB/fault.
ple_read_fusion.caveat: the 891 t/s build already runs this unfused path, so it is not the current bottleneck - it is a standing cost at 16 rows/token, and a transferable optimization we have already validated once.
ple_read_fusion.why_adjacent_merging_will_not_help: lookups are hash-derived over 16 heads x ~20M rows each; at 16384 tokens that is a density of ~1/1221, so sorted neighbours average ~110 KB apart and same-page collisions are ~3.7%. Merging adjacent ranges - what our Vulkan path does - barely fires here.
ple_read_fusion.what_would_help: the page cache holds 4 KiB pages of which we use 90 bytes, so ~20 GB of free RAM caches only ~0.44 GB of useful rows. Unbuffered reads (FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING) plus our own row-granular userspace cache would let the same RAM hold ~45x more rows.

page_cache_dominates_prefill.finding: RETRACTED as stated - see upstream_head_b0f31f58_20260917.retracted. The cold-vs-warm swing was a cross-binary artefact. Whether cache state matters for one binary is unmeasured.
page_cache_dominates_prefill.mmap_verdict: RETRACTED: -lzm on is 4.2x slower not because mmap is bad but because load_lazy_reader returns nullptr unless lazy.mode == LLAMA_LAZY_MODE_DIRECT (llama-model.cpp:1867), so qwen4exp_ple_prefetch early-returns and there is NO prefetch and no concurrency at all. Vulkan reads the same ~3.2 KB per lookup as HIP (380 t/s x 16 x 3289 B = the same 20 MB/s), so read amplification does not distinguish the two paths.
page_cache_dominates_prefill.carve_tension: the 96 GB carve raised prefill (783 -> 880) but cut system RAM 63 -> 31.6 GB, which is what starves the PLE cache. These pull in opposite directions and the balance has never been measured.
page_cache_dominates_prefill.hypothesis_for_the_pwilkin_gap: a smaller carve leaves enough RAM to hold the whole 28.8 GB table resident, i.e. permanently in our warm state. Testable in BIOS.

ple_io_concurrency_20260917.finding: the PLE gather runs at ~10% of the concurrency it is configured for; the SSD is not the limit
ple_io_concurrency_20260917.cause: each worker does read_at then GetOverlappedResult(..., TRUE), so it holds exactly one outstanding I/O; gather() also spawns and joins its workers on every call, once per ubatch.
ple_io_concurrency_20260917.fix: keep several requests in flight per worker (or IOCP / ReadFileScatter) and reuse a persistent worker pool. Costs no RAM, unlike the userspace row cache.
ple_io_concurrency_20260917.supersedes: the row-cache proposal is NOT the first lever: that trades RAM for I/O, but the I/O is not saturated.
ple_io_concurrency_20260917.also_explains: the 4x cold/warm prefill swing - cold means real disk reads, and that path runs at 10% efficiency. Fixing concurrency should narrow the swing on its own.
ple_io_concurrency_20260917.caveat: counters sample at ~1 s while the gather is bursty, so 6.1 is a busy-window average and a lower bound on burst concurrency; the independent Little's law figure of 6.8 agrees.

ssd_ceiling_20260917.tool: tools/ssd_random_read.py (buffered reads against the model GGUF, server unloaded)
ssd_ceiling_20260917.gather_vs_ceiling: the depth-16 PLE gather does 262034 rows in 2.284 s = 114727 IOPS, i.e. 97.5% of that peak. The depth-1 gather did 84965 IOPS = 72%. So the unfused path IS at the practical ceiling of this access pattern: 262144 page reads cannot take less than ~2.23 s without reducing the NUMBER of reads.
ssd_ceiling_20260917.what_that_costs: that 2.23 s is 12.3% of a pp16384 run at 903 t/s (18.1 s). Removing it entirely is worth ~1030 t/s.
ssd_ceiling_20260917.caveat_512b: a 512-byte run measured 142203 IOPS at depth 16, but Python reads are buffered so the device still faults 4 KiB pages - that number is application-level and does NOT demonstrate a device-level win. Proving it needs FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING.
ssd_ceiling_20260917.suspicion: 482 MB/s of random 4 KiB is low for this class of NVMe, so the ceiling we hit is likely the Windows cache-manager fault path rather than the drive - which is the argument for unbuffered sector-granular reads plus our own row cache.

vulkan_ple_fusion_mechanism.what_it_actually_does: llama_mmap_row_pages maps each row index to its page(s), sorts, dedups at PAGE granularity, merges consecutive pages into ranges, and prefetch_rows hands ALL ranges to a single PrefetchVirtualMemory call (one posix_madvise per range on POSIX). It is not one read per 8 rows - it is one batched submission, which is what lifts the queue depth.
vulkan_ple_fusion_mechanism.bytes_are_the_same: Vulkan reads ~3289 B per lookup (380 t/s x 16 lookups vs the reported 20 MB/s) against HIP's measured 3245 B. Read amplification does not distinguish the two backends; only submission batching and concurrency do.
vulkan_ple_fusion_mechanism.where_the_8_could_come_from: a 4 KiB page holds ~45 rows of 90 B; a 512 B sector holds ~5.7. Unbuffered sector-granular reads would be the 8x, not the page-merging path. Unproven - see ssd_ceiling_20260917.caveat_512b.

blocker_resolved_20260918.what_it_really_is: the Windows commit limit, not the kernel. This box has 31.6 GB visible RAM and an automatically managed page file (94.2 GB allocated, max ~3x RAM), so the commit limit is 123.6 GB. A server at ctx 262144 / ub 8192 with MTP commits 91.5 GB at prefill peak (device allocations from the 96 GB carve are charged to the process), and the whole system sits at 126.3-127.4 GB while the page file expands - allocations that land faster than the expansion get std::bad_alloc ('bad allocation').

evidence.repeats_ctx262144_55k_prefill: IQ3_S runtime 4 fails / 8 runs (bad allocation, always right after the fourth 8192-token ubatch), production runtime 0 / 7 - both peaking at 91.2-91.7 GB process commit and 126.3-127.4 GB system commit (tools/memwatch.ps1)
evidence.repeats_ctx131072: IQ3_S runtime 3 / 3 pass at 792-831 t/s, process commit peak 84.4 GB, system commit 122.3-123.4 GB (under the limit)
evidence.gates_off_do_not_matter: LLAMA_MMB_GLU=0 and FASTLLM_NO_SIGMOID_FUSE=1 fail the same way; the IQ3_S kernel is not the allocator

blocker_resolved_20260918.also_found: LLAMA_MMB_CACHE=0 crashes outright: mmb_cache_insert() erases g_mmb_cache.front() when size() >= 0 on an empty vector (mmb.cu:640). Unsupported value, pre-existing.
fix_options: set a fixed page file (initial = max, e.g. 160 GB on C:, 1.1 TB free): lifts the commit limit and removes the expansion race; needed for the PRODUCTION runtime too, which passed its runs 0.5 GB under the ceiling
or reduce the carve (96 -> 80 GB): more visible RAM raises the automatic page file max and keeps the PLE table resident
or run ctx 131072 (-7 GB of commit)

halogen_changelog_leads_20260917.how_halogen_handles_UD_IQ4_XS_at_1400: 0.7.0 - it repacks EVERY tensor losslessly at load and never requantizes, covering IQ4_NL / IQ4_XS / IQ3_S / Q4_0 experts, Q8_0 trunk and Q6_K output, then caches the repack to disk (HALOGEN_GGUF_CACHE, 70 GiB, ~5 min; later starts 1.4 s warm / 16 s cold). actionable.expert_ordering_counting_sort: 0.5.3 - 'Expert ordering produced by general-purpose sort...counted out directly instead', worth +4.6% at 8k, +8.1% at 32k, +7.9% at 128k. Ours is mm_ids_route_sort in mmid.cu: a 1024-element BITONIC sort per chunk (55 stages, a __syncthreads each), run once per 1024 routes - 160 chunks for a 16384-token prefill at 10 used experts. A counting sort over the 512 experts replaces it with one histogram, a 512-wide scan and one scatter.
actionable.ple_gather_concurrency: 0.6.3 - reading the lookup table one row at a time (28 MB/s) cost 46-52 s on a 32k prompt; reading 64 rows at once (HALOGEN_NGRAM_GATHER_THREADS - threads, i.e. concurrency, not contiguity) cut it to 1.3 s. Our gather already uses 64 workers and now 16-deep overlapping, but theirs is ~3.6x faster per row (524288 rows in 1.3 s against our 262144 in 2.28 s).
actionable.prompt_lookup: 0.6.0 - n-gram speculation off the request's own context, +15% on coding-agent decode (49.1 -> 56.3 tok/s). manager.py already wires --spec-type ngram-mod but it has NEVER been measured on HIP.

expert_counting_sort_attempt_20260917.attempt: replaced it with a counting sort: histogram into shared counts, a 512-wide ping-ponged inclusive scan, then a scatter through an atomic per-expert cursor. Same contract for mm_ids_route_scatter (keys contiguous per expert, starts[e] the run start, counts[e] its length).
expert_counting_sort_attempt_20260917.why: caching the expert ids in LDS (so global memory is read once rather than once per pass) bought only +2 t/s, so the cost is not the loads: it is the atomic cursor serialising threads that land on one expert, plus a 512-wide scan that costs more than the sort it replaces. The bitonic version runs entirely in LDS with no atomics, which suits 1024 elements. halogen's gain must come from their own ordering code, not this shape.

unbuffered_sector_reads_20260917.question: a PLE row is 90 bytes and a 4 KiB page holds ~45 of them while we use one, so would FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING with 512-byte sector reads cut the cost 8x?
unbuffered_sector_reads_20260917.tool: tools/ssd_unbuffered_read.py (CreateFileW with FILE_FLAG_NO_BUFFERING | FILE_FLAG_RANDOM_ACCESS, sector-aligned buffers, server unloaded)
unbuffered_sector_reads_20260917.verdict: NO. 512-byte reads are only +12% in IOPS, not 8x. The drive is IOPS-limited, not bandwidth-limited: it serves ~110-124k operations per second whether each moves 512 B or 4 KiB. Smaller reads buy nothing, so the unbuffered sector-granularity plan is dead.
unbuffered_sector_reads_20260917.what_it_redirects_to: the cost is the NUMBER of operations, and the way to cut that is cache hit rate. The page cache stores 4 KiB pages holding ~45 rows each, of which a random lookup uses one, so ~20 GB of free RAM caches only ~5M useful rows. A row-granular userspace cache at 90 bytes would hold ~222M rows in the same RAM - 44x - which against a 320M-row table is roughly a 69% hit rate instead of the 21% measured today, cutting disk operations ~2.5x and the gather from 2.28 s to about 0.9 s.
unbuffered_sector_reads_20260917.explains_halogen: their 0.6.3 figure of 524288 rows in 1.3 s is 403k rows/s, well ABOVE this drive's ~124k IOPS ceiling, so most of their lookups must be cache hits - they run a smaller carve and have far more system RAM. It is not a faster drive.

what_limits_decode_20260917.what_is_left: the node count itself. 7325 nodes per forward pass over 48 layers is ~153 per layer, i.e. ~5.5 us of GPU time per node at 40.6 ms per token. Even replayed from a graph at zero CPU cost, each is a kernel that must launch and drain on the GPU, and at batch 1 each does very little work - which is exactly a compute graph that rises and falls without filling.

node_census.reading: only 16.1 MUL_MAT and 3.0 MUL_MAT_ID per layer do real arithmetic; ADD/MUL/SCALE/UNARY together are 51.6 per layer of elementwise work that is pure overhead at batch 1. That is where fusion pays.

what_limits_decode_20260917.lever: operator fusion to cut the node count - the same thing journey steps 06-10 did (fused HC combine+norm, fused gate GEMM + stream mix, gated rms-norm, depthwise conv1d). A well-fused layer should be 20-40 nodes.
what_limits_decode_20260917.tool: LLAMA_GRAPH_TRACE=1 on the HIP build prints graph usage, re-capture rate and a one-shot node census
what_limits_decode_20260917.CORRECTION: the earlier entry read the graph's 7325 nodes as 7325 kernels. Instrumenting the dispatch loop shows 2331 actually dispatch per pass; 3853 are swallowed by existing fusions and 1141 are views/noops. So per-kernel time is 17.4 us, not 5.5, and weight traffic alone accounts for ~14.5 ms of the 40.6 ms step at best-case bandwidth. Kernel count is still the lever but the headroom is smaller than first stated. The MoE expert-sum ADD chain singled out as the fattest target is ALREADY fused by ggml_cuda_op_moe_weighted_reduction.

mxfp4_on_gfx1151_20260917.question: a LocalLLaMA post reports Qwen3.8 27B NVFP4 at 5809 t/s prefill / 276 t/s decode on an AMD R9700 via an MXFP4 fast path - does that help us?
mxfp4_on_gfx1151_20260917.answer: NO. The R9700 is RDNA4 (gfx1201); this machine is gfx1151, RDNA3.5. Probed by compiling the WMMA builtins with the SDK's own clang: on gfx1151 __builtin_amdgcn_wmma_f32_16x16x16_f16_w32 compiles (so the probe is sound) while the fp8 and fp4 variants do not exist. There is no hardware FP4 or FP8 matrix path on this chip.
mxfp4_on_gfx1151_20260917.consequence: MXFP4 weights here would have to be dequantized to bf16 and fed through the same F16 WMMA that MMB already uses for IQ4_NL - the format itself buys nothing. MXFP4 is ~4.25 bpw against IQ4_NL's 4.5, so even the memory-traffic saving is marginal.
mxfp4_on_gfx1151_20260917.also_not_comparable: that post runs a 27B model; ours is 177B. Its absolute numbers say nothing about this one.

qsa_verification_leak_fix_20260918.what: root cause of the MTP/n-gram 'answer stops mid-sentence' reports: speculative verification batches leaked their own draft tokens into the target through unmasked dense attention, once the context was long enough for QSA to be active (> indexer_top_k + r - 1 keys, ~2K tokens)
mechanism: LLAMA_QSA_NO_DENSE_MASK=1 (the maskless trial) builds the QSA attention op with block indices and no kq_mask; only the qsa3 kernel (ggml-cuda/qsa.cu) applies the selection itself, and it declines q->ne[1] < 128

on HIP ggml_cuda_flash_attn_ext_mma_f16_shall_use_sparse() is CUDA-only and returns false, so every batch qsa3 declines ran the generic flash-attention kernels: dense attention over the whole cache with NO causal mask

single-token decode has nothing to leak; a 2-8 token verification batch lets the target's logits at token i see tokens i+1.. = the drafts they verify. Acceptance stops being a check, the text drifts toward the 4B MTP head, loops, and ends on <|im_end|>

decode_vs_context_20260918.tool: tools/decode_vs_context.py: growing prefixes of one random-word document with cache_prompt on, 64 greedy tokens per depth, spec off, production runtime
decode_vs_context_20260918.reading: decode is NOT context-independent on HIP: +23.5 ms from 2K to 97K. About half (0.13 ms per 1K tokens, ~12 ms at 97K) is the attention op itself: on HIP the sparse indices are honoured only by the qsa3 kernel (>= 128 queries), so a 1-token batch runs the generic kernel over the whole 12-layer f16 cache (24 KB per context token: 12 attention layers x 2 KV heads x 256 x K+V x f16 = 2.3 GB at 97K). The other half (0.118 ms per 1K, ~11 ms at 97K) is the selection path that also scans the cache: indexer scores, relu-sum, top-k, score bounds and mask work. By design (top_k 2048 blocks) both should be flat; the fix is a decode-side sparse path on HIP (gather the selected blocks, ~50 MB, then attend) and a profile of the selection ops at depth.

qsa3_small_batch_force_20260918.implication: a small-batch sparse path is real work, not a gate flip: either a persistent packed K/V cache maintained incrementally (like the GDN write-through), or a decode-side gather of the selected blocks from the raw cache (get_rows on a [1024, n_kv/4, n_head_kv] block view per query + a tiny position mask) feeding the standard flash-attention kernel with the queries as the batch dimension (~16 MB per layer per token instead of the whole cache).

decode_depth_ablation_20260918.method: tools/decode_vs_context.py --words 700,28800 --n 64 (2.3K and 97.5K context), spec off, 64 GB carve (absolute numbers slow, slopes valid), FASTLLM_SKIP_OPS zero-fills one op class per run

slope_ms_per_1k_ctx.GET_ROWS: invalid (7.6 s/token: zeroed row indices break the graph)

decode_depth_ablation_20260918.reading: the attention op is exactly half of the context slope (0.308 -> 0.154); none of the selection ops (indexer, top-k, argsort, softmax) or the copies carry the other half. The remaining 0.154 ms per 1K tokens (~15 ms at 97K) is in something the class ablation cannot isolate - candidates: the indexer-score MUL_MAT over all cached index keys (a skinny GEMV whose kernel may run far below bandwidth), or host-side per-token work proportional to n_kv. FASTLLM_NODE_TIMING (per-dispatch stream events, bin/hip-rocm101-timing) is the tool for the rest.

decode_node_timing_97k_20260918.tool: FASTLLM_NODE_TIMING=1 (+ GGML_CUDA_DISABLE_GRAPHS=1) in ggml-cuda.cu: stream events around every dispatch, per-kind totals printed after each graph; bin/hip-rocm101-timing
decode_node_timing_97k_20260918.reading: the second half of the context slope is the indexer block-key rebuild: every graph gathers ALL cached raw indexer keys (GET_ROWS over 97536 rows), mean-pools them into 24384 blocks, rms-norms and ropes every block - per decoded token. That is O(context) work whose inputs never change for a completed block. Fix: cache the finished block keys (patches/apply_qsa_block_key_cache.py, bin/hip-rocm101-kb) and build only the blocks a ubatch completes. The other half (FLASH_ATTN_EXT running dense) needs the decode-side sparse path.

user_84k_matrix_20260918.what: the user's own 82155-token prompt run end to end on the production server (spec off, ctx 262144, ub 8192), carve x trunk-precision matrix
reading: the 96 GB carve is worth +13% prefill and +40% decode on a real 84K workload; 64 GB is not a viable carve for this model

the Q6_K decode twins are FREE on prefill at 96 GB (856.7 vs 854.0) and worth -4% decode ms (56.12 vs 58.49). At 64 GB they cost 7% prefill (703.9 vs 752.6) because the 2.9 GB lands in an already spilling carve. Enable the switch only where the carve has room.
decode at 84K is 58.5 ms against 39 ms at 2K on the same build: the context slope dominates a long chat, which is what the block-key cache and a decode-side sparse attention path are for
user_84k_matrix_20260918.user_observation: parallel > 1 makes the server use shared GPU memory; parallel = 1 does not. Reproduced by the user across restarts; the cause is not yet identified (KV and recurrent state are the same size either way under -kvu).

qsa_block_key_cache_20260918.what: a finished QSA block's indexer key depends only on its member cells and its position, so it is built once, when a write completes the block, into one F16 row per indexer cell (plus a scratch row) and read back afterwards. Before it, every graph rebuilt every block key from the whole cache: gather all raw keys, mean-pool into n_kv/4 blocks, rms-norm and rope them, per decoded token.
qsa_block_key_cache_20260918.cost: one F16 [128, kv_size+1] tensor per indexer layer = 12 x 64 MiB at ctx 262144

quality.note: both identical to production; 600 greedy tokens byte-identical; 6/6 multi-turn with MTP + n-gram at 28.4-31.6 tok/s

qsa_block_key_cache_20260918.reading: at 97K the cache is worth 5.1 ms/token (+8.7%: 17.11 vs 15.74 tok/s) and cuts the context slope by a quarter. Short context is unchanged (the first graph after any position move still rebuilds everything). Prefill 950.7 t/s and batch-1 decode 38.88 ms are both at production level.
qsa_block_key_cache_20260918.bug_that_cost_the_evening: an incremental graph reads no blk_cells / blk_pos (its keys come from the dirty list), so ggml never allocates them - but set_input_qsa_impl still filled them, writing through a null data pointer. It died as an access violation inside VCRUNTIME's memset with no message; the Windows Application Error log named the faulting module and settled it after four wrong hypotheses. Rule: any graph input that some graph variant stops reading must be treated as optional in set_input.

qsa_decode_gather_20260918.patch: patches/apply_qsa_decode_gather.py (models/qwen4exp.cpp); LLAMA_QSA_DECODE_GATHER=1 enables, set with the other QSA gates by manager.py; LLAMA_QSA_DECODE_GATHER_MAX_T caps the batch size (default 8)
qsa_decode_gather_20260918.what: decode-sized batches gather the ~2051 selected cells out of the K/V caches into a compact pair, pad to a multiple of FATTN_KQ_STRIDE, mark -1 entries and the padding with a -inf mask, and run the ordinary flash-attention kernel over 2304 keys instead of the whole cache. No packed layout and no extra memory, unlike feeding the qsa3 kernel.
qsa_decode_gather_20260918.why_not_qsa3: QSA3_FORCE=1 lifts the kernel's q->ne[1] < 128 gate but the packed K/V operands (src[6]/src[7]) are only built under layout_prefill (n_tps >= 128), so the predicate still declines: measured as a null test (PPL, token equivalence and the context slope all unchanged). Giving the kernel those operands at decode would mean maintaining a packed copy of the whole cache, +6.4 GB at ctx 262144.
qsa_decode_gather_20260918.numerics: decode becomes sparse, matching the model's design and what prefill already does; NOT bit-identical to the dense decode it replaces

quality.note: prefill untouched; six-turn MTP + n-gram 6/6 at 28.4-30.1 tok/s

qsa_decode_gather_20260918.gate: the cache must be at least twice the padded selection: gathering 2304 of 2329 cells measured slower than reading them in place (42.9 vs 41.1 ms at 2.3K)
qsa_decode_gather_20260918.combined_with_block_key_cache: 97K decode went 63.54 -> 47.91 ms/token today (15.74 -> 20.87 tok/s, +33%), and the context slope 0.241 -> 0.078 ms per 1000 tokens. Prefill 963.7 t/s and batch-1 decode 38.45 ms are at production level.
